editorNote: July reviews put adventure, affordable applications and the online meter on the home-computer desk.
morningLine: SSI trades the battlefield for the cavern; Atari readies a summer challenger.

lead.headline: SSI ventures into arcade adventure with Gemstone Warrior
lead.dek: A war-game specialist sends Apple and Commodore players underground.
body: Strategic Simulations Inc., best known for detailed war games, is trying a different sort of battle. James V. Trunzo’s July COMPUTE! review finds Gemstone Warrior an arcade-oriented adventure in which fast decisions and quick reflexes matter more than the patient calculations of a historical simulation. This is a current review, not a claim that the game first appeared this week.

The assignment is to recover five fragments of a stolen magical gemstone from 90 underground caverns. A crossbow-armed warrior confronts monsters and gathers magical objects along the way. Knowing when to use those devices is as important as keeping the weapon pointed in the right direction.

The review covers Commodore 64 with a disk drive and the Apple II series with at least 48K and a disk drive. A joystick is optional, but recommended. Several difficulty levels let players adjust the challenge, while a pause feature offers relief from the action.

A successful expedition can run as long as two hours, making the ability to save a game in progress more than a convenience. Trunzo calls SSI’s first true arcade entry impressive: an invitation for home-computer adventurers to explore a publisher normally associated with a very different battlefield.

stories.headline: Atari prepares the ST for summer buyers
body: Atari’s 520ST is approaching its summer test with buyers. In his July COMPUTE! column, Tom R. Halfhill describes hands-on time with the machine and a development-lab tour led by Sam and Leonard Tramiel. The earlier April availability promise has slipped; U.S. quantity availability is now expected in summer, with Europe receiving earlier shipments.

The production model has 512K RAM, but its initial operating system, GEM and programming language load from disk rather than ROM. Halfhill reports about 240K free after loading. The planned $799 package includes system disks, a microfloppy drive and a high-resolution monochrome monitor refreshing at 70 Hz; that is a reported package plan, not a verified dealer offer this week.

Atari also promises a sub-$500 10MB hard disk by fall and a sub-$500 CD-ROM peripheral by year end. Those remain promises. Across the Atlantic, the July 4 Popular Computing Weekly reports a revived proposal for a 256K 260ST with a built-in drive, while the Amiga’s U.S. unveiling is still ahead on July 23.

stories.headline: HomePak bundles writing, filing and telecommunications for $49.95
body: Batteries Included is making an inexpensive bid for the everyday home-computer desk. Sheldon Leemon’s July COMPUTE! review examines Russ Wetmore’s HomePak: HomeText for writing, HomeFind for filing and HomeTerm for telecommunications, at $49.95 for the reviewed Atari and Commodore package.

The package requires an Atari 400/800, XL or XE with at least 48K and disk drive, or a Commodore 64 with disk drive. A printer and modem are recommended. None of its three programs is copy-protected. IBM PC, Enhanced Model PCjr and Macintosh versions are described as forthcoming; the future Macintosh package is listed at $69.95.

HomeTerm supplies XMODEM transfers, an online-time counter, macros and an outgoing edit window that keeps half-written replies separate from incoming conference text. Memory is a constraint: Atari HomeText and HomeTerm buffers hold about 7K, roughly three double-spaced pages, with somewhat larger buffers on Commodore. The first Commodore HomeTerm cannot dial the 1650 modem; the review describes a free disk-return update for original owners.

stories.headline: The online information boom comes with a running meter
body: The modem can lead to a local hobbyist board or a professional information service, but the bill changes dramatically with the destination. July COMPUTE! distinguishes BBSs, commercial information services and specialist databases. A BBS often costs only the telephone call, although some boards charge membership fees to support operation and manage demand.

CompuServe, The Source, Dow Jones News/Retrieval, Delphi and American People/Link offer a growing menu of quotations, reference material, conferences and newspaper archives. The article gives commercial-service costs ranging broadly from $5 to $100 or more per hour, with specialist databases reaching $300 to $400. These are category ranges, not a quoted rate for any one named service.

Arlan R. Levitan’s Telecomputing Today column offers a practical countermeasure: write mail before connecting. Fifteen minutes spent typing online can cost a couple of dollars, and even a free board may entail a long-distance call. Local user groups can help newcomers learn the territory before the meter starts.

storeShelves.label: Top 5 Computer Games — editorial selections, not sales rankings
items: Spelunker — $29.95 in Steve Hudson's July review, p. 52. Brøderbund; reviewed for Commodore 64 and Atari with disk drive and joystick. Six increasingly challenging levels, scrolling caverns, batteries, flares and dynamite; a current review, not a newly verified release.
Gemstone Warrior — SSI arcade-adventure review, pp. 55–56; see lead. Price omitted because OCR is unclear.

Run For It — Karen McCullough reviews Weekly Reader Family Software's robot maze game, p. 52 onward. Apple II or Atari with 48K and disk; 72 rooms in 18 levels. Robot Orbit gathers energy and avoids hostile devices.

The Goonies heads for UK shops — PCW July 4, p. 1 says US Gold plans to import Datasoft's film-based computer game in September. UK film release is described as Christmas; retain regional distinction and future tense.

A View to a Kill — Domark advertisement in PCW July 4, p. 8 claims availability on Spectrum 48K, Commodore 64 and Enterprise; Amstrad and MSX are future versions. p. 12 profiles developer Tigress. Advertisement claims, not independently verified stock.

periodAd.headline: Bond on the home screen
periodAd.summary: Domark’s July 4 Popular Computing Weekly advertisement claims A View to a Kill availability for Spectrum 48K, Commodore 64 and Enterprise, with Amstrad and MSX versions to follow. These are advertisement claims, not an independently checked stock report.
periodAd.tagline: The licensed adventure visits the keyboard.

market.headline: Summer competition meets the household budget
market.summary: Atari’s planned $799 ST package and HomePak’s $49.95 review price illustrate competing bids for the home-computer budget. British reports of Acorn rescue talks and uncertainty over a proposed Sinclair takeover show the pressure on the other side of the counter.

worldAnchor.headline: Freed TWA hostages reach West Germany
worldAnchor.summary: The July 1 Guardian reports that all 39 remaining hostages left Damascus for Frankfurt after their June 30 release. President Reagan welcomed their freedom while noting that seven other kidnapped Americans remained in Lebanon.

bbsNote.headline: Write first, connect later
bbsNote.summary: Online time and long-distance calls make preparation worthwhile; HomeTerm brings a timer and an outgoing edit window to the home desk.

posts.text: Levitan recommends composing mail offline to reduce connect-time and long-distance charges.
The July review describes an outgoing edit window, online timer and XMODEM transfers.
Popular Computing Weekly reports plans to expand through the remainder of 1985 after early teething troubles.

curiosity.headline: A robot sings to the wastebasket
curiosity.summary: Fred D’Ignazio finds personality more compelling than household utility.
curiosity.detail: In July COMPUTE!, the columnist describes HEROjr reciting nonsense rhymes, mistaking pets for humans, ordering hamburgers from a bathroom sink and singing Old MacDonald Has a Robot to a wastepaper basket. These are his playful descriptions of robot behavior. The same page captions Tomy’s remote-controlled Omnibot 2000 at about $500.

gadgetWatch.summary: The July 4 Popular Computing Weekly reports a legal dispute over Amstrad’s dual-cassette tape-copying machine.
